name: Pitjantjatjara
confidence_why: Every description of Pitjantjatjara, from the grammars of Rose 2001 and Langlois 2004 to the instrumental study of Tabain, Fletcher and Butcher 2014 and the dissertation of Wilmoth 2023, puts primary stress on the first syllable of the word; the only open point is secondary stress, which the older descriptive tradition places on odd non-final syllables and on disyllabic suffixes but which Tabain, Fletcher and Butcher 2014 could not detect phonetically and Wilmoth 2023 leaves unresolved.
catalog_quote: analyses presented in Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher (2014) show that the first syllable of the Pitjantjatjara word is marked by a raising of pitch and by extra duration, but that there is no evidence for secondary stress elsewhere in the word.
sweep_summary: Two works with stress in the title. (1) Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher 2014 'Lexical stress in Pitjantjatjara' (J. Phonetics 42:52-66, doi 10.1016/j.wocn.2013.11.005): the primary instrumental study, directly about word stress in this language, but closed access everywhere checked (Unpaywall closed; OpenAlex closed, no repository fulltext; Semantic Scholar CLOSED with abstract elided; ScienceDirect 403; no archived copy at the Internet Archive); Harvard the Harvard library catalogue online access exists. Priority high. Its conclusion is already known second-hand from the authors' held JIPA Illustration (2014:198, the catalog's deciding quote, verified verbatim): initial syllable marked by raised pitch and extra duration, no evidence of secondary stress. (2) Glottolog's 'Rose 2005, Negotiating kinship: interpersonal prosodies in Pitjantjatjara (Word, 22pp)' resolves via Crossref to Rose 2008, word 59(1-2):189-215 (doi 10.1080/00437956.2008.11432586); its abstract, recovered from an Internet Archive copy of the paywalled T&F page and saved, shows a systemic-functional study of MOOD, MODAL ASSESSMENT and kinship exchanges -- 'prosody' in the SFL sense, silent on word stress; priority none. Re-read held/on-disk sources for the record: Rose 2001:112 and Langlois 2004:30-31 (first-hand: primary stress on the first syllable; Langlois adds secondary stress on di-/polymoraic suffix-initial vowels), Wilmoth & Mansfield 2021:11-12 (confirms) and Wilmoth 2023:88-89 (refines: Tabain et al. labelled strict SWSW alternation, so secondary stress on disyllabic suffixes remains open). classification: the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding and deciding source stand; no new source supersedes it.

new_statements.quote: Pitjantjatjara does not differ from this description and the initial vowel has primary stress. In the case of verbs prefixed by a directional prefix, both the prefix and first syllable of the verb have primary stress. [maa-pitja 'AWAY-go', ngalya-pitja 'THIS.WAY-go'] In case of dimoric and polymoric suffixes, the initial vowel of the suffix receives a secondary stress. [wangka-nytji-kitja 'talk-NOML-INTENT']
new_statements.citation: Langlois, Annie. 2004. Alive and Kicking: Areyonga Teenage Pitjantjatjara. Pacific Linguistics 561. Canberra: ANU. §2.3.2 'Stress', pp. 30-31.
new_statements.reading: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word (each directional prefix and its verb stem count as separate stress domains); the descriptive tradition adds secondary stress on the initial vowel of di-/polymoraic suffixes and on odd non-final syllables. This is the clearest first-hand descriptive statement read in this search of works with stress in the title, but it belongs to the impressionistic tradition whose alternating secondary stresses the instrumental study (Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher 2014, restated in the held JIPA 2014 p.198) failed to confirm. Nothing read here moves the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding; the only live nuance remains whether disyllabic suffixes carry secondary stress (Wilmoth 2023:88-89 keeps it open). Neither of the two works with stress in the title yields a new first-hand statement: the J. Phonetics article is closed-access, and Rose 2005/2008 is SFL mood/modality, silent on word stress.

new_statements.quote: Pitjantjatjara and other Western Desert languages have been described as having stress in the following locations (by, for example, Douglas, 1957 [...] Rose, 2001): • Primary stress on the first syllable of the prosodic word (directional prefixes and reduplicants constitute their own prosodic word); • Secondary stress on odd numbered syllables thereafter; • Secondary stress on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes; • Final syllables do not bear stress. [...] Tabain et al. (2014) found several phonetic correlates strongly associated with word-initial primary stress, but no evidence for secondary stress.
new_statements.citation: Wilmoth, Sasha. 2023. The Dynamics of Contemporary Pitjantjatjara: An Intergenerational Study. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's fixed initial-syllable coding (initial stress) and with the existing Langlois 2004 statement; adds the bimoraic (quantity-sensitive) foot analysis, the prefix/reduplicant-as-separate-prosodic-word domain, and the explicit statement that secondary stress on disyllabic suffixes is unresolved after Tabain et al. 2014. Note that the stress-placement list on p. 88 is a summary of earlier descriptions (Douglas 1957.. Rose 2001), whereas the p. 131 statement on prefix/root primary stress and the bimoraic-foot analysis are Wilmoth's own.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the prosodic word; a directional prefix (ma-, ngalya-, para-, wati-) or a reduplicant is its own prosodic word and carries its own primary stress, so prefixed/reduplicated verbs carry more than one primary stress (p. 131: 'Both the verbal root and the preceding directional prefix/reduplicant will receive a primary stress'). Feet are bimoraic, built left to right, so a long initial syllable forms a foot on its own ((táan)(tjaka)-ṉi, p. 89-90); final syllables are unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The descriptive tradition puts secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables and on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes (p. 88). Wilmoth reports that Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher (2014) found no phonetic evidence for secondary stress, but argues (p. 88-89) that their labelling assumed strict SWSW alternation rather than suffix-sensitive footing, so 'the question of whether disyllabic suffixes bear secondary stress remains open for further research in my view' (p. 89). She keeps the metrical 'reset' by disyllabic suffixes, reduplicants and compounds on independent morphological evidence (p. 90, pp. 142-143), 'even if they receive no secondary stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Directional prefixes and reduplicants are separate prosodic words with their own primary stress (pp. 88, 131); disyllabic suffixes reset footing and can leave word-medial unfooted syllables, e.g. (tjáa)ta(-mila)-ṉi (p. 91); ma- is written short but pronounced long so as to meet the bimoraic word minimum (p. 131). No lexical exceptions to initial primary stress are mentioned. Wilmoth notes that stress and vowel length 'are described as being very uniform among all varieties' of Western Desert (p. 88).
new_statements.identity_note: Wilmoth 2023 describes contemporary Pitjantjatjara as spoken at Pukatja (Ernabella) and nearby APY communities, comparing younger and older speakers with earlier descriptions; she states that stress and vowel length are described as very uniform across Western Desert varieties (Pitjantjatjara, Yankunytjatjara, Ngaanyatjarra, Pintupi), and her §4.2.3 discussion explicitly contrasts Pitjantjatjara with the Pintupi description of Hansen & Hansen 1969/1978 that the theoretical literature has used. Blake 1991 is a pan-Australian introduction listing Pitjantjatjara among eleven reference languages; not opened.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees about primary stress, which every description places on the first syllable of the prosodic word. The one live disagreement concerns secondary stress: the descriptive tradition summarised by Wilmoth 2023 p. 88 (Douglas 1957, Goddard 1985, Langlois 2004, Rose 2001, etc.) posits secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables and on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes, whereas the instrumental study Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher 2014 (the catalog's deciding source, known here via the JIPA 2014 restatement) found no phonetic evidence for secondary stress. Wilmoth 2023 pp. 88-89 argues that Tabain et al. tested strict SWSW alternation rather than suffix-sensitive footing and that the question of secondary stress on disyllabic suffixes 'remains open'; she retains bimoraic feet and metrical reset on morphological evidence regardless. This does not affect the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding. Blake 1991 could not be opened, so it neither confirms nor contradicts.

sources.citation: Langlois, Annie. 2004. Alive and Kicking: Areyonga Teenage Pitjantjatjara. Pacific Linguistics 561. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: Most commonly in Australian languages, primary stress (ˈ) goes onto the first syllable of the word. There is then often secondary stress (ˌ) on the third, fifth etc. syllables, excepting that the final syllable of a word does not usually bear stress (Dixon 1980:128). Pitjantjatjara does not differ from this description and the initial vowel has primary stress. In the case of verbs prefixed by a directional prefix, both the prefix and first syllable of the verb have primary stress. [...] In case of dimoric and polymoric suffixes, the initial vowel of the suffix receives a secondary stress.
sources.note: First-hand descriptive statement: primary stress on the initial vowel; both a directional prefix and the verb's first syllable carry primary stress; secondary stress on the initial vowel of dimoric/polymoric suffixes (and, following Dixon, on 3rd/5th syllables, never final). Confirms initial primary stress; posits the secondary stresses that the instrumental study did not find.

sources.citation: Rose, David. 2001. The Western Desert Code: An Australian Cryptogrammar. Pacific Linguistics 513. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: A foot begins with a stressed syllable, the Ictus, followed by a weak syllable, Remiss (see Abercrombie 1967). There is a very close complementarity in Western Desert between the foot and the word. Almost every word in the language is spoken with the stress on the first syllable, both in isolation, as in Figure 2.21, and in larger structures of group and clause.
sources.locator: §2.5.3 'Stress wave', p.112 (the text); summary at ch.2 p.29 (line 1039)
sources.note: First-hand: almost every word is stressed on its first syllable; a foot = stressed an earlier reading + Remiss (+ one or two enclitic syllables); multisyllabic suffixes can be spoken on a dependent foot (p.29 summary). Confirms initial primary stress.

sources.citation: Tabain, Marija, Gavan Breen, Andrew Butcher, Anthony Jukes & Richard Beare. 2016. Stress Effects on Stop Bursts in Five Languages. Laboratory Phonology 7(1): Art. 16, pp. 1-23. doi:10.5334/labphon.38
sources.quote: Pitjantjatjara and Warlpiri both have stress on the first syllable. Tabain, Fletcher, and Butcher (2014) have shown that in Pitjantjatjara, stress is encoded by duration, a word-tone on the first syllable, and possibly by loudness. There is little evidence for vowel reduction, and there is no evidence for secondary stress in the language. [...] For Pitjantjatjara, as was seen in our previous study, there are large lengthening effects for /c/ and /k/, and a lesser lengthening effect (trend) for /p/. For the apicals however, the difference is not significant. [...] /k/ has a lower CoG in Strong syllables (approaching significance at p = 0.003), while the neutralized apical /T/ has a higher CoG in Strong syllables (though this is only significant compared to /ʈ/).

tone.quote: Pitjantjatjara has a left-headed binary foot structure, with final syllables treated as extra-metrical [15]. Primary stress is word-initial and initial/stressed syllables are strongly associated with a pitch peak which shows significantly longer duration than other syllables in the word. We are specifically interested in the F0 height of H tonal targets associated with accented syllables in Pitjantjatjara clause-chains.
tone.summary: No lexical tone; intonational H targets sit on word-initial stressed syllables and are downstepped linearly across a clause chain within one Intonational Phrase, with final lowering at the IP end.

Australasian Speech Science and Technology Association (ISSN 1039-0227).

tone.quote: Like most Australian indigenous languages, Pitjantjatjara has been analysed as a stress language [4, 5]. Like all Australian languages analysed to date, it can be further assumed that Pitjantjatjara also makes use of intonation to mark out “chunks” of speech. [...] The –H tone in Pitjantjatjara is effectively a left-edge demarcative tone which contributes to the perception of main word accent in this language. [...] Another factor that clearly supports this interpretation is that in our corpus there are no word-medial prominence-lending rises that would suggest anything other than a demarcative word accent.
tone.locator: p. 213, sec. 1 Introduction (first part); p. 216, sec. 4 Discussion (second part)
tone.summary: No lexical tone: Pitjantjatjara is analysed as a stress language whose pitch events are post-lexical/intonational -- a demarcative H word accent (-H) at the left edge of each phonological word, peaking in the word-initial (main-stressed) syllable rhyme, plus phrase-level and IP-final boundary tones (H-, L-, H%, L%).

sources.quote: The goal of this paper is to give the the first reader sense of the rich varieties of discourse through which speakers of the Australian language Pitjantjatjara enact their social relations. The brief sketch here is based on a fuller survey in Rose 2001, using the tools of systemic functional linguistics (SFL) for relating language to its social contexts. The discussion involves three steps: firstly, an outline of the options for enacting interpersonal meanings in Pitjantjatjara, in its systems of MOOD and MODAL ASSESSMENT, secondly, an outline of the system of social relations in Pitjantjatjara culture, governed by the kinship system, and finally, examples of exchanges between various kin
